sentences.text: In 2024, the influence index stands at 31.6 for China (band 23.0–65.2, from 3 of six components) and 16.4 for the United States (band 13.9–65.2, from 4 of six components). The net lean is +15.2 points toward China.
Over the five years to 2024, the index for China rose by 5.2 points and the index for the United States rose by 4.3 points.

The value for China rests on trade export share, trade import share and diplomatic alignment; every component is a recorded tie (trade shares, finance, debt, UN votes, legislative stance), not a judgement.

The value for the United States rests on trade export share, trade import share, finance flow and diplomatic alignment; every component is a recorded tie (trade shares, finance, debt, UN votes, legislative stance), not a judgement.
In 2025, 7.9% of Colombia's mineral exports (UN Comtrade value US$6.1 bn) went to China and 24% to the United States; together 32%, the rest to other destinations.
Since 2020 the share going to China was broadly flat and the share going to the United States fell by 8.0 points.
Relative to the twelve-country export basket, its exports are specialised in nickel (RCA 7.5) and gold (RCA 5.1).

5 sudden shifts in export shares are flagged from the customs data, the latest in 2018: Exports to the United States fell from 44% to 24% of the country's mineral exports between 2017 and 2018 (reported by COL to UN Comtrade).
AidData records US$1.4 bn of documented commitments from Chinese institutions to Colombia over 2003–2021 (55 events; the source ends in 2021).
The DFC and OPIC records show US$1.7 bn of documented commitments from US institutions to Colombia over 1989–2026 (250 events).

The lenders with the largest recorded commitments to named recipients here are OPIC (predecessor of DFC) (US$668 m), US International Development Finance Corporation (US$544 m) and China Development Bank (CDB) (US$462 m).
In the UN General Assembly, voting agreement in 2024 was 78% with China and 39% with the United States.
Since 2019, agreement with China was broadly flat and agreement with the United States rose by 9.2 points.
Too few mineral-related legislative records naming either actor have been scored for a stance series (five per year are needed); the text model is zero-shot baseline, not yet validated.

After Executive Order 13817: A Federal Strategy to Ensure Secure and Reliable Supplies of Critical Minerals (2017-12), the share of exports to the United States moved -25.6 points (48% before, 22% after); placebo p 0.17 against the series' other years (event list still in draft). An association, not a cause.

After Section 301 tariffs on imports from China, first tranche in force (2018-07), the share of exports to the United States moved -19.2 points (46% before, 27% after); placebo p 0.25 against the series' other years (event list still in draft). An association, not a cause.

After Section 301 tariffs on imports from China, first tranche in force (2018-07), the share of exports to China moved +8.0 points (6.9% before, 15% after); placebo p 0.08 against the series' other years (event list still in draft). An association, not a cause.

The published forecast for the share of mineral exports going to China in 2030 is 6.6% (90% band 0.0%–23%), from random walk with drift, which beat naive persistence by 4% CRPS in backtests; the last observed year is 2025.

The published forecast for the share of mineral exports going to the United States in 2030 is 25% (90% band 0.0%–57%), from naive persistence, because no model beat it in backtests; the last observed year is 2025.
The published forecast for the influence index of China in 2030 is 30.7 (90% band 21.1–44.0), from naive persistence, because no model beat it in backtests; the last observed year is 2024.

The published forecast for the influence index of the United States in 2030 is 11.0 (90% band 0.0–27.7), from damped local linear trend (Kalman filter, maximum likelihood), which beat naive persistence by 6% CRPS in backtests; the last observed year is 2025.
Under the stated scenarios the 2030 median share to China ranges from 0.0% (US sourcing rules bite) to 17% (accelerated China pull); these are what-ifs with a fixed yearly shift, not predictions.

In 2025, unavailable components: legislative stance (no scored legislative records naming the actor); debt stock (no source for debt owed to the United States); finance flow (source coverage ends 2021); debt stock and diplomatic alignment (source coverage ends 2024).

Source coverage ends at different years: Chinese official finance to 2021, US finance to 2026, debt by creditor to 2024, UN votes to 2024 and trade to 2025; components beyond a source's coverage are unavailable, not zero.
12 of the dated events used above are still in the draft event list awaiting the project owner's review.
Stance values come from the text model (zero-shot baseline, not yet validated); the rest of this brief rests on official statistics and the registered databases, each cited on its chart.

human.text_md:
## Alignment

Colombia is the exception to the regional pattern. Of US$6.1 bn of mineral exports in 2025, 24% went to the United States and 7.9% to China; gold, US$5.1 bn of the total, went US$1.4 bn to the United States and US$29 m to China [concentration:share_us_x:2025] [concentration:share_cn_x:2025] [flow_trade:COL:gold:2025]. Documented commitments are also balanced: US$1.1 bn from Chinese institutions and US$1.1 bn from the DFC over 2015–2021, then US$252 m from the DFC in 2022–2024 [flow_finance:CN:COL:2015-2021] [flow_finance:US:COL:2015-2021]. The index still leans toward China, 31.7 against 16.4 in 2024, because the components beyond trade (UN voting, Chinese debt) pull that way [index_value:influence:CN:2024] [index_value:influence:US:2024]. My reading: Colombia's mineral ties run to the United States and its index runs to China, which says the index measures recorded ties of several kinds, not trade alone.

## Trajectory

The Chinese share of exports has never been large: 12% in 2008, 5% in 2016, 10% in 2020, 8% in 2025 [concentration:share_cn_x:2008] [concentration:share_cn_x:2025]. The nickel and copper that do go to China (US$274 m and US$174 m in 2025) are the exceptions inside a gold economy [flow_trade:COL:nickel:2025]. Five sudden trade shifts are flagged [anomaly_flag:sudden_trade_shift]. The window after the 2017 US critical-minerals order shows the share to the United States falling 26 points and the share to China rising 8, a gold-market movement that no US policy explains [event_effect:us_eo13817_critical_minerals:US:window:COL] [event_effect:us_eo13817_critical_minerals:CN:window:COL]. The twelve coded statements are too few for a pooled stance; the two by US officials are both negative on China [statement:count:COL] [statement:count:bloc=United States:COL]. The legislature's coded records are sparse and positive toward both powers in 2020 [document:stance_cn:COL:2020].

## Risks and likely next moves

The models keep China's share under 17% in 2030 in every path and the US share at 24% at baseline and 34% under reshoring [forecast:export_share:CN:china_pull:2030:COL] [forecast:export_share:US:us_reshoring:2030:COL]. There is no parity gap to close [insights:parity_gap:COL]. My reading: the mineral question in Colombia is copper and nickel at the margin, not gold; the risk to the US position is a copper project whose offtake goes to China, which would show first in the copper row.

## What would change this reading

A copper or nickel export row to China above the gold flow to the United States; Chinese commitments above the 2019 level; or coded statements in enough number to score the executives.
